Keelwater · Senior PM task
The roadmap towards agentic claim handling
Customers ask for automatic sorting. What they're buying is speed they can trust.
Michelle Muller October 2026
01 · The brief
The brief, as I understand it
Keelwater: claims software for ~180 enterprise insurers. Handlers spend most of their day in it. Assumption: focus on car and motor claims.
How sorting works today
A handler puts every new claim in one pile.
New claim
Simple · pay it quickly
Needs a closer look · check first
Suspicious · investigate
The pressure
Existing customers want sorting automated, and a competitor has launched it.  Deals in the pipeline are waiting on it. Consistent ask from CS and sales. 
A top-10 account renews in 5 months. That gives us a timeline to aim for: 5 months.
The constraints
Every claim decision must be explainable to the customer and the regulator.
Before anything automated goes live, each customer's IT and AI governance teams must approve it. Regulations differ by country. 
Current status
Bulk sorting that's half done ships in 6 weeks.
Data-team prototype, shelved 18 months ago. 
01 · The brief
The answer up front
The problem
Insurers want to process and pay honest claims faster without risking fraud, and be able to explain every decision.
The recommendation
Now: bulk sorting, so handlers can select many claims and sort them in one go
Next: rule-based automation learned from handler actions: pile suggestions, missing-information flagging, advanced filtering
Later: workflows that chain the automations into an end-to-end sequence
What we tell Sales and CS
Bulk sorting is the first release towards agentic automation.

01 · The brief
The evaluation set strategy
Every phase generates evaluation sets. Working this way builds the harness (skills and tools) alongside the evals.
Every action is labelled ground truth
Bulk sorting, auto-suggestions and workflows each record the ground truth and what the handler did. The labels are golden answers: what the correct sort was.
They accumulate into an evaluation harness
The harness guides the agent and validates every change to it.
No evaluation sets, no production-ready product
Robust datasets of ground truth are non-negotiable before go-live.
Stages 1, 2 and 3 build towards:
The agent that can sort claims,  which is made of:
Skills · how to act
Tools · to operate
Evals · what good looks like
Why agents are high-risk in insurance
Highly regulated: bad agent actions mean fines, lawsuits and regulatory violations
Full explainability required on every agent action
The agent doesn't know what good looks like. Neither does Keelwater. The customer does.
01 · The brief
The signal: what it tells us, and what it doesn't
What we know
£2.3M ARR
6 open deals mention it, incl. the biggest in the pipeline
3 accounts
raised it in reviews; one top-10 renews in 5 months
~40 tickets
in 6 months; several large customers asked directly
1 competitor
launched automatic sorting last quarter
What we don't: 
What "automatic" looks like: are these suggestions a handler confirms or is there no human in the loop? Is the goal to stop at sorting or continue to processing completion?
The exact pain: claimant speed, headcount, inconsistent sorts, or a competitive checkbox? Is it mainly for the "simple" majority or the slow 15%? Is that consistent across all customers?
How concentrated: ~40 tickets across ~180 customers is low. Is this concentrated from a few accounts or the whole base? What is the profile of these customers?
Whose pain: handlers use Keelwater, but is this coming from them or heads of claims, ops, IT teams  who are likely the buyers?
Where fraud fits: should sorting catch fraud, or is that just one feature to consider?
The competitor: what it actually offers, and whether buyers would consider swapping platform just for this capability 
02 · The data
The facts the brief gives us
2.1M claims a year
~175k a month; ~11.7k per customer a year
11 min median
time to sort: most claims aren't slow
15% over 4 hours
~315k claims a year
3.4% re-sorted
within 30 days, ~71k a year: the human baseline
What doesn't add up
An 11-min median from arrival includes queue time. It only works if claims are picked up around the clock.

02 · The data
The slow tail is stuck claims
Claims over 4 hours are waiting on
48% the claimant
28% a third party
15% injury details
6% a fraud check
Assumption: There's no "waiting on claimant" status, so handlers leave these claims unsorted.
So: a waiting-on-claimant status and missing-information flagging could be cheap, early wins that would speed up the sorting process.

The questions I'd ask, and how I'd collect the answers
A clear sense of the problem
  • Main problem per customer?
  • Why do some claims take hours?
  • Full lifecycle, sorted to paid?
  • Which way do re-sorts go?

  • Must every sort be right, or is some error OK?
  • Same for every customer, or configurable?

  • What's in the shelved prototype?
  • What fraud checks do customers run?

02 · The data
Facts, gaps, assumptions: what they mean for the need
Fact from the brief, and the gap
What I assumed
What it changes about the need
15% take over 4h. Why?
Waiting on claimant 48%, third party 28%, injury 15%, fraud 6%. No "waiting" status.
Stuck claims, not fraud. Cheap, early wins
~180 customers. All the same?
Segments: simple-heavy 55% of claims, mixed 33%, complex-heavy 12% (A-07)
No single global model: per-insurer rules and thresholds
~40 tickets. Saying what?
22 of 40 are about sorting many claims at once; 3 customers filed 18
Bulk sorting answers a real, concentrated pain
6 deals "mention" it. Buying what?
Speed, fraud still caught, an expert in the loop. Most have a fraud vendor.
Sell speed you can trust: suggestions a handler confirms
Explainable. To what standard?
By region: NAIC (US), UK GDPR 22A–D, FCA Consumer Duty. Records, human review
A selling point, and no LLM making the decision
Bulk sorting ~12 weeks. Why?
No table view today; handlers sort one claim at a time
The foundation: suggestions need a table to appear in
Shelved prototype. What is it?
Gradient-boosted model, public sample data, rule-made labels; never tested on real claims
A concept for customer sessions, not a shortcut
Sources: assumptions log, internal data, customer signal, examiner requirements.

04 · The solution
The bulk sorting decision
The options
1 · CHOSEN
Ship it as the validation layer for automation
2
Don't ship: pause it and move the squad onto automation, since that's what the deals are asking for
Decision
Ship bulk sorting, and add to it:
1 Build it to capture and label every customer action
2 Iterate quickly to show value from the "waiting on claimant" and "missing information" statuses
Why
Real ticket demand: 22 of 40 tickets are about sorting many claims at once
No table view today: handlers sort one claim at a time
3 beta customers lined up, incl. the top-10 renewal
It produces what automation needs: the filters handlers use become the first rules; their bulk actions become labelled data

05 · Safe and valuable
How we know it's safe
Reduce the surface area of uncertainty: use the LLM to find patterns in how handlers already decide, and keep it away from the decision itself.
Rules come from handlers' own decisions
"You sorted 41 windscreen claims under £1,000 with no third party as Simple." A human accepts each rule, so every sort traces back to a person.
The LLM finds patterns and extracts; it never decides
It reads free text into fields, quoting the source. The decision is rules plus the insurer's fraud score: explainable by construction.

06 · GTM and Customer Success
What we tell Sales and CS, and when
Bulk sorting is the first release towards agentic automation.
Every sort your handlers make teaches the system what good looks like, and builds the evals that make each step up safe and explainable to your regulator.
Week 1
Sales and CS leads
Holding message: we've heard it, here's how we're finding out what buyers need. Ask AEs and CSMs the discovery questions
Weeks 2–3
Commercial, tech, design
Findings and release path shared async, then a Q&A in one room
Week 6
Rollout and get design partners from release 2-3
Bulk sorting launch; PM and CSM lead implementation sessions and continue to validate direction
Release 2
Design partners: gradual release
Suggestions pilot on their own claims
Release 3
Workflows
Per-insurer workflows with design partners, including the top-10 account before renewal
Never promise: automatic payment or denial, our own fraud detection, dates beyond release 1 before the tech lead agrees them
Assets: battle card, objection handling, a vendor evidence pack for governance teams, generated from the repo

07 · How I used AI
Where AI got it wrong
Where AI got it wrong
What it affected
How I caught it
What we learn
Defined the middle pile as "information missing", the largest category
Fact sheet, research, assumptions: the wrong pile
Reading: it didn't match my brainstorm; a search on motor triage confirmed it
A wrong framing compounds. Check definitions early. Missing info became a status
Stated "fraud is the blocker" as fact
The strategy would have been a fraud model
Brainstorming: I asked to test it before building on it
Test the framing before the solution
Invented per-customer data with complex-heavy insurers as the biggest
Segment sizes; who to pilot with
Reading: totals matched the brief, not how the market works
Invented data can add up and still be implausible
Listed "above authority limit" as a cause of slow sorting
The cause split and decision order
Reading: I asked what it meant and why it was there
Whole-journey research doesn't always fit the step you measure
The middle-pile error would have changed the product. Fixing it is how missing information and awaiting claimant became a status on any claim in any pile and quick(ish) win. 
07 · How I used AI
How the product lifecycle is changing
Discovery compresses
Thematic analysis of calls and tickets takes hours, not weeks. The bottleneck moves to asking the right questions and checking the answers.
Prototypes become the spec
A clickable prototype with tests in a day: validate with customers before committing the squad.
Judgement and reading become the job
Every error on the last slide was caught by me reading or using the output.
Decisions have to be explicit
AI writes fluently enough that unmade decisions look made.
What I'd prioritise at Keelwater
A shared context hub (calls, tickets, research, decisions) that agents and people both use
Evals and audit trails in the definition of done
The same human-in-the-loop discipline for ourselves that we ask of insurers' handlers
